text: In classical computing, copying data is so basic it barely registers as a feature — it's just assignment, Ctrl+C. Quantum mechanics forbids the equivalent operation outright, for an unknown state, and it forbids it provably, not just practically.

The no-cloning theorem says: no unitary operation takes an arbitrary, unknown qubit state together with a blank qubit and produces two independent copies of it, for every possible input state. If you already know exactly which state you have, copying is trivial — you just prepare a second one from that knowledge. What's forbidden is copying a state whose identity you don't already know.

Suppose such a universal cloning unitary existed. It would have to clone the basis states correctly: ket-zero ket-zero stays ket-zero ket-zero, and ket-one ket-zero becomes ket-one ket-one. Because U must be linear, applying it to ket-plus — ket-zero plus ket-one, over root 2 — forces the output to be ket-00 plus ket-11, over root 2: an entangled Bell state. But a correct clone of ket-plus should be ket-plus tensor ket-plus, which expands to all four coefficients equal to 0.5 — a completely different state. U can't satisfy both basis cloning and linearity and produce a correct clone. Contradiction. No universal cloning machine exists.

This proof used nothing about current technology — no noise, no decoherence, no qubit count. It used only two structural facts: that quantum operations must be linear, and that a correct clone of a superposition must be a clean product state. Better engineering will never close this gap, because it isn't an engineering gap — it's a theorem about what linear operators can and cannot do, in the same category as 'you cannot divide by zero.'

Notice the attempted clone of ket-plus didn't fail by doing nothing — it produced something real, just not a clone: an entangled state. This is a recurring pattern — operations that would be impossible as clean duplication often succeed instead at entangling the two systems. And you can't measure your way around it either: extracting full information about an unknown state via measurement collapses it, destroying the original superposition just as surely as cloning would have. Every piece of classical infrastructure relies on copying being free and perfect — none of that intuition transfers to an unknown qubit.
Next lesson works out exactly what this means in practice: for error correction, for checkpointing, and for detecting an eavesdropper trying to intercept a quantum channel.
